turns_text: [SEG0001] person_1 (DOCTOR): Come, sit, both of you. The fan in that waiting room is useless, I know. What brought you in today?
[SEG0002] person_2 (PATIENT): This cough. Dry. It is spoiling my sleep and I am frankly irritated, doctor, we waited a long time.
[SEG0003] person_3 (FAMILY_MEMBER): He was coughing the whole night again. I told him we should have come earlier, but he—
[SEG0004] person_2 (PATIENT): I can talk, no? Don't start. It is a dry cough. Nothing is coming out.
[SEG0005] person_1 (DOCTOR): Okay. Tell me in your own time, how long has the cough been with you?
[SEG0006] person_2 (PATIENT): Three weeks. Well, actually, maybe a little over that. It came after a cold.
[SEG0007] person_3 (FAMILY_MEMBER): It is a month. I am the one awake, I know. From the start of last month, not three weeks.
[SEG0008] person_2 (PATIENT): It is not one month. After the cold only. Three weeks. You are stretching it.

[SEG0009] person_1 (DOCTOR): So one of you says three weeks, the other says about a month. I will keep it as somewhere between three weeks and a month, we don't have to fight the calendar. The cold you mentioned, what was that like?
[SEG0010] person_2 (PATIENT): Running nose, few days, sneezing. Then the nose stopped and this dry cough sat down and stayed. I still think it is the cold only, the tail of it.
[SEG0011] person_1 (DOCTOR): And the runny nose, that part is finished now?
[SEG0012] person_2 (PATIENT): Finished. Gone. Only the cough.
[SEG0013] person_3 (FAMILY_MEMBER): When he coughs hard he gets short of breath. Stairs also, he slows down, I have seen it.
[SEG0014] person_2 (PATIENT): I do not get short of breath. I am tired, that is separate. Stop adding a new disease every sentence.

[SEG0015] person_1 (DOCTOR): Tired, we will come to. On the breathing, you are saying it is not there, she is saying it is there with the cough and the stairs. I am leaving that one open, I won't push you.
[SEG0016] person_2 (PATIENT): Good, because it is not there. I am tired because the cough wakes me up. Two, three times a night. That is the whole story.
[SEG0017] person_1 (DOCTOR): Any fever in these weeks, even a mild one?
[SEG0018] person_2 (PATIENT): Mm, I suppose... sometimes, not really. I didn't put a thermometer. I don't know what you want me to say.
[SEG0019] person_3 (FAMILY_MEMBER): One evening he felt warm to my hand. Last week. I thought fever.
[SEG0020] person_2 (PATIENT): You thought. I was not feverish. It was a hot room. Leave the fever.
[SEG0021] person_1 (DOCTOR): Alright, I am not writing down a fever from a warm room and a maybe. Chest pain? Any whistling in the chest?
[SEG0022] person_2 (PATIENT): No chest pain. No whistling, no wheeze. Just a tickle in the throat and this cough.
[SEG0023] person_1 (DOCTOR): And phlegm, anything you are bringing up?
[SEG0024] person_2 (PATIENT): Mm, I suppose, sometimes, not really. Mostly it is dry. I would say dry. Can we move on, my head is heavy from not sleeping, not from pain.
[SEG0025] person_3 (FAMILY_MEMBER): He has BP since many years, doctor. And there is a new tablet.

[SEG0026] person_2 (PATIENT): Yes, pressure is long-standing, many years. They put me on ramipril recently. When exactly, I cannot tell you the date. Last month, six weeks, something. I don't keep a diary.
[SEG0027] person_1 (DOCTOR): That is fine, dates can stay fuzzy. What strength of ramipril are you on?
[SEG0028] person_2 (PATIENT): Five milligrams. One in the morning.
[SEG0029] person_3 (FAMILY_MEMBER): The box in the drawer is ten milligrams, I read it yesterday. Ramipril 10. He mixes it up.
[SEG0030] person_2 (PATIENT): I am not mixing it up. It is five. Or... the pharmacy foil looked different. I still say five. I take one tablet in the morning, that much I know.
[SEG0031] person_1 (DOCTOR): Then I will not lock in a dose when the two of you are reading different foils. Are you taking it every morning, or are some mornings missed?
[SEG0032] person_2 (PATIENT): Most mornings. Sometimes I forget if I am late for the bus. Not a big thing.
[SEG0033] person_3 (FAMILY_MEMBER): It is two or three mornings a week, doctor. I count the tablets. He will not admit it.
[SEG0034] person_2 (PATIENT): It is not two or three. Sometimes. I take my medicine. Drop it.
[SEG0035] person_1 (DOCTOR): So the intention is daily, and whether the misses are rare or frequent, we actually don't know. Any other medicine for the pressure, or for anything else?

[SEG0036] person_2 (PATIENT): There is the water tablet. Small white one. For the swelling— no, for the BP. The old doctor gave it years back. I still take one in the morning. The name, I cannot tell you. Don't make me guess.

[SEG0037] person_3 (FAMILY_MEMBER): Also, my brother takes lisinopril for his pressure. I wrote it on a paper because the chemist said it is the same family. It is his tablet, not my husband's. My brother has had high BP for years.
[SEG0038] person_1 (DOCTOR): Thank you, we will not put your brother's lisinopril on your husband's list. High BP in the brother is worth knowing. Did you take anything for the cold or the head?

[SEG0039] person_2 (PATIENT): Crocin, when the head was paining at the start. Not every day. Four times, five times, in these weeks, I think. Cold is gone so I stopped the Crocin. I am not taking it now.
[SEG0040] person_1 (DOCTOR): Crocin meaning paracetamol, yes, and it is stopped. Any allergy to a medicine, swelling of the lips, rashes?
[SEG0041] person_2 (PATIENT): No. No allergy. I can take what you give.
[SEG0042] person_3 (FAMILY_MEMBER): He has never smoked. Alcohol also no, he will have tea only, too much tea. We stay together, I am home most of the day.

[SEG0043] person_2 (PATIENT): The tea is not a medical problem. Can you tell me what this cough is? I have a cousin's wedding on Sunday and I cannot be coughing into the microphone, he has asked me to speak.

[SEG0044] person_1 (DOCTOR): Wedding we will not solve, but let me examine you. Lean forward... breathe normally. Lungs are clear. I am not hearing a wheeze, and no crackles. Your throat looks mildly irritated, that is all.
[SEG0045] person_1 (DOCTOR): Pressure today is 152 over 94. Pulse is 88, regular. You don't feel hot, I am not recording a temperature because I did not measure one.
[SEG0046] person_2 (PATIENT): 152 is the waiting room, doctor. At home it is better. Usually. I think.
[SEG0047] person_1 (DOCTOR): Clinic readings do sit higher sometimes. Around the time the cough started, had the ramipril already been started, or was it the other way round?

[SEG0048] person_2 (PATIENT): They changed my old BP tablet to ramipril around the same time as the cold. I cannot separate the dates. I keep thinking the cough is the cold. Maybe the tablet. I don't know.
[SEG0049] person_3 (FAMILY_MEMBER): The old one was amlodipine, five milligrams. They stopped it the day ramipril was started. I was in the room.
[SEG0050] person_2 (PATIENT): Yes, amlodipine, stopped. I was comfortable on that one. This ramipril I am not fond of, but don't ask me to swear it is the cause.
[SEG0051] person_1 (DOCTOR): You are still taking the water tablet alongside, yes?
[SEG0052] person_2 (PATIENT): Yes. Morning. One. Name is gone from my head. Some long name, white, small. That is all.

[SEG0053] person_1 (DOCTOR): Let me think out loud, and you can stop me if I wander. A dry cough lasting weeks, starting near the time of ramipril, is something this family of tablets can do, and it is also very possible this is just the cold dragging its feet, which is what you have felt from the beginning. I am not making a firm diagnosis of the cough today, either explanation stays open.
[SEG0054] person_2 (PATIENT): So after all this you are saying maybe, maybe not. I could have stayed home.

[SEG0055] person_1 (DOCTOR): I am saying I won't label it, but I will change the drug. Stop the ramipril from today, I don't want an ACE inhibitor continued while the cough is unexplained. Instead we will use telmisartan, forty milligrams, one tablet every morning, by mouth.
[SEG0056] person_2 (PATIENT): Forty milligrams. And I keep the water tablet? My wife will lose the box, she loses everything.

[SEG0057] person_1 (DOCTOR): Keep the water tablet, same as now, until we identify it. Bring the strip or the old box next visit, whichever you find. Telmisartan forty milligrams by mouth each morning, not your brother's lisinopril. Please don't borrow from relatives.
[SEG0058] person_3 (FAMILY_MEMBER): I want an x-ray. My neighbour had a cough and it was something bad, I keep thinking.

[SEG0059] person_1 (DOCTOR): I understand the worry. I am not arranging a chest x-ray today. If the cough has not settled three weeks after the ramipril is stopped, then we might do a chest x-ray. Not booked now.
[SEG0060] person_2 (PATIENT): Neighbour stories. Everyone has a neighbour. Fine. Three more weeks of this.

[SEG0061] person_1 (DOCTOR): Often the cough eases after the ACE tablet is gone, and often it was the virus all along. I am not promising which. If you get chest pain, or breathlessness that is new, or you bring up blood, don't wait for me, come earlier.
[SEG0062] person_3 (FAMILY_MEMBER): He has also been very low. Not talking, irritable with everyone. Is the BP doing that?
[SEG0063] person_2 (PATIENT): I am irritable because I am tired and the waiting was endless. I am not depressed. Don't put me on some mood tablet now.
[SEG0064] person_1 (DOCTOR): I am not calling this depression, and no mood tablet. Broken sleep will make anyone snap. You sound tired, which matches what you told me, not a new label.
[SEG0065] person_2 (PATIENT): Good. So the only change is the BP tablet?

[SEG0066] person_1 (DOCTOR): Stop ramipril, start telmisartan forty milligrams every morning by mouth, continue the unnamed water tablet, and come back in three weeks. I want that review anyway, to see the cough and recheck the pressure. Reception outside will put the date on a card, but the plan is three weeks from today.
[SEG0067] person_3 (FAMILY_MEMBER): And if the cough is the same at that visit, the x-ray?

[SEG0068] person_1 (DOCTOR): If it is not better in three weeks, we consider the chest x-ray at that same visit. I am not ordering any blood tests today, there is nothing I need from a lab this afternoon.
[SEG0069] person_2 (PATIENT): If I feel worse before three weeks I am not sitting and counting days.
[SEG0070] person_1 (DOCTOR): Then you come sooner. The booked review is still in three weeks, whether you needed an earlier visit or not.
[SEG0071] person_2 (PATIENT): My wife's brother and his lisinopril, she already said. Just so you don't write that under my name by mistake. I have never taken lisinopril.
[SEG0072] person_1 (DOCTOR): It is not going on your prescription. Telmisartan is a different class. Less often linked with cough, though that is not me declaring ramipril guilty.
[SEG0073] person_3 (FAMILY_MEMBER): We have a BP machine at home. Should he use it?
[SEG0074] person_1 (DOCTOR): Yes, if you are willing. A couple of quiet morning readings, write them down, bring the paper. I am not treating today's decision from numbers we haven't seen.
[SEG0075] person_2 (PATIENT): I will write, if I remember. Don't expect a full chart. I am not a clinic.
[SEG0076] person_1 (DOCTOR): Rough notes are enough. Any swelling in the feet now, or any change in how you pass urine, with that water tablet?
[SEG0077] person_2 (PATIENT): No swelling. Urine is as usual, normal. I don't even know why that tablet is still in my life.
[SEG0078] person_3 (FAMILY_MEMBER): Years back his feet had swollen, that is why they added it. Not recently. He forgets that part.
[SEG0079] person_2 (PATIENT): Years back, maybe. Not now. And my head is not paining today, before you ask again. Can we wind up? The parking fellow was already shouting.

[SEG0080] person_1 (DOCTOR): No headache today, good, and we won't restart Crocin unless you actually get pain. You stopped it, leave it stopped. Bring the water-tablet strip, stop ramipril tonight, start telmisartan tomorrow morning. I will see you in three weeks.
[SEG0081] person_3 (FAMILY_MEMBER): I will keep the strips in my purse. And I will watch the morning dose, even if he glares at me.
[SEG0082] person_2 (PATIENT): I can glare and still take a tablet. I am tired, not helpless. Are we done?
[SEG0083] person_1 (DOCTOR): We are done. Go carefully in that traffic, and if something frightens you before the three weeks, just come back, don't phone around the family first.

spec.situation: Hypertension patient with a dry cough for weeks that they connect to 'a cold'; recently started ramipril or enalapril; they mention a relative's lisinopril. Doctor thinks aloud, changes the drug but does not give a firm diagnosis of the cough.
features: third_party_medicine: someone mentions a medicine or condition that belongs to a relative or friend (the sister's biotin, the husband's metformin). It must not appear as the patient's own; a relative's illness can only be family history if said as such.

colloquial_drug_names: medicines referred to by colour, purpose or brand ('the water tablet', 'Crocin', 'my sugar tablets', 'the purple inhaler'); the name is recorded as said, the normalized name only if it is clear.
relative_speaks_for_patient: a relative answers for the patient and the patient partly contradicts; reported_by follows who said it.
ambiguous_answer: an answer that sounds like yes but is really 'maybe' ('mm, I suppose', 'sometimes, not really'); recorded with uncertainty or not at all, never as a firm fact.

bad.reason: Transcript says brother, not brother-in-law, has high BP.
Family member reports one warm evening last week, but resolution status is not stated.
bad.text: feeling warm (category=constitutional, status=resolved, onset=one evening last week, temporality=resolved, reported_by=family_member, certainty=disputed)

bad.reason: Transcript mentions brother, not brother-in-law, regarding lisinopril.

omissions.text: Ramipril current dose was not established and should not be implied as known; patient said 5 mg each morning, family member said the box was 10 mg, and the doctor explicitly did not lock in a dose.
Ramipril had been started recently, around last month to six weeks ago, replacing amlodipine around the same time as the cold/cough began.
Patient reported possible very occasional sputum but said the cough is mostly dry ('sometimes, not really; mostly dry').
Negative finding: no current shortness of breath according to the patient, despite the family member's concern.
Negative finding: no current fever was accepted by the doctor; only an unmeasured disputed feeling of warmth was discussed.
Negative finding: no swelling of the lips or rash with medicines was denied as part of allergy history.
Negative finding: no change in urination with the water tablet.
Doctor did not measure a temperature and specifically said none was being recorded.
Past history detail for the water tablet: it was originally added years ago because of foot swelling, not recently.
Family history is recorded with the wrong relation: it was the family member's brother (the patient's brother-in-law) who has hypertension and takes lisinopril, not the patient's brother.
The patient has never taken lisinopril; it belongs to the relative and should not be attributed to him.
Plan detail missing: no blood tests were being ordered that day.
Follow-up purpose missing: the 3-week review was specifically to reassess the cough and recheck blood pressure.
